entry: Mental disorder characterized by [[Hallucination|hallucinations]] (typically hearing voices), [[Delusion|delusions]], disorganized thinking or behavior, and flat or inappropriate affect. Symptoms usually begin in young adulthood, and there is no objective diagnostic test. Males are more often affected and have an earlier average onset. Causes include genetic and environmental factors, such as [[Cannabis (drug)|cannabis use]] during adolescence. About half of those diagnosed improve over the long term without further relapses, while the rest have lifelong impairment. Average life expectancy is reduced by 20 to 28 years, and the suicide rate is about 5% overall. Treatment centers on antipsychotic medication, with counseling, job training and social rehabilitation. Clozapine is offered when initial antipsychotics fail.

Mental disorder characterized by thought disorder, paranoia, [[Anxiety|social anxiety]], derealization, transient [[Psychosis|psychosis]] and unconventional beliefs. Affected people often feel strong discomfort in forming social connections, believing that others hold negative views of them, and paranormal or superstitious beliefs are common. The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM-5) classifies it as a [[Personality disorder|personality disorder]] in cluster A, while the ICD-11 places it among psychotic disorders. Those affected usually disagree that their thoughts are a disorder. It occurs in about 3% of the general population and is more often diagnosed in males.

Coastal state of northern Germany, the northernmost of its sixteen states, comprising most of the historical Duchy of Holstein and the southern part of the former Duchy of Schleswig. Its capital is Kiel, and it borders [[Denmark|Denmark]] and the city-state of [[Hamburg|Hamburg]]. The Danish king ruled both duchies from 1460, and the resulting dispute became known as the Schleswig-Holstein Question. Prussia and Austria won the Second Schleswig War in 1864, and Prussia absorbed the territory in 1867. Plebiscites in 1920 returned Danish-speaking North Schleswig to Denmark. Its economy includes shipbuilding and trade around the [[Kiel Canal|Kiel Canal]], fishing, and offshore wind energy.

Partial differential equation governing the [[Wave function|wave function]] of a non-relativistic quantum-mechanical system. Austrian physicist [[Erwin Schrödinger]] postulated it in 1925 and published it in 1926. It is the quantum counterpart of Newton's second law in classical mechanics, giving the evolution over time of the wave function of an isolated system. Schrödinger built on [[Louis de Broglie]]'s proposal that all matter has an associated matter wave, and the equation predicted the bound states of the atom in agreement with experiment. Because it contains a first derivative in time and a second in space, it is non-relativistic. [[Paul Dirac]] later combined [[Special relativity|special relativity]] and quantum mechanics in the [[Dirac equation]]. Other formulations include matrix mechanics, introduced by [[Werner Heisenberg]], and the path integral formulation, developed chiefly by [[Richard Feynman]].

Thought experiment in quantum mechanics devised by physicist [[Erwin Schrödinger]] in 1935, in discussion with [[Albert Einstein]]. A cat in a sealed box, linked to a random subatomic event, may be considered simultaneously alive and dead while unobserved. Schrödinger intended it to criticize the views of [[Niels Bohr]] and [[Werner Heisenberg]], which he saw as leading to absurd conclusions. It is often used to discuss the measurement problem, which asks when a [[Quantum superposition|superposition]] ends and reality resolves into one outcome. Superposition has been observed in very small objects, but a cat would pose considerable technical difficulties.

Paramilitary organization under [[Adolf Hitler]] and the [[Nazi Party]] in Nazi Germany and German-occupied Europe. It began as a small guard unit in Munich. [[Heinrich Himmler]] joined in 1925 and directed it from 1929 to 1945, when it became the foremost agency of security and terror. Its Allgemeine SS enforced racial policy, and the Waffen-SS was its combat arm. Its Death's Head units ran the concentration and extermination camps, and the SS was most responsible for the genocide of an estimated 6 million Jews during the [[The Holocaust|Holocaust]]. The [[Nuremberg trials|Nuremberg tribunal]] later judged the SS and the Nazi Party to be criminal organizations.

Parameter in the Schwarzschild solution to [[Einstein field equations|Einstein's field equations]] that corresponds to the radius of a black hole's event horizon, given by rₛ = 2GM/c², where G is the [[Gravitational constant|gravitational constant]], M the mass and c the [[Speed of light|speed of light]]. German astronomer Karl Schwarzschild calculated the solution in 1916. Every mass has a Schwarzschild radius, which is proportional to the mass. The Sun's is about 3.0 km (1.9 mi), Earth's about 9 mm (0.35 in) and the Moon's about 0.1 mm (0.004 in). An object whose radius is smaller than its Schwarzschild radius is a [[Black hole|black hole]].

Pain going down the leg from the lower back. About 90% of cases are due to a spinal disc herniation pressing on a lumbar or sacral nerve root. Other causes include spondylolisthesis, spinal stenosis, piriformis syndrome, pelvic tumors and [[Pregnancy|pregnancy]]. Imaging is usually unnecessary unless bowel or bladder function is affected. In about 90% of cases, symptoms resolve in less than six weeks. Initial treatment is usually pain medication, although evidence for its effectiveness is lacking. If severe pain lasts more than six weeks, [[Surgery|surgery]] may be an option, but its long-term benefits are unclear.

Genre of speculative fiction that imagines advanced and futuristic changes in [[Technology|technology]], scientific knowledge or biological systems. Its common elements have grown from [[Space exploration|space exploration]], extraterrestrial life and time travel to parallel universes, dystopian societies, information technology and transhumanism. Subgenres include hard science fiction, which emphasizes scientific accuracy, space opera, and [[Cyberpunk|cyberpunk]], which explores the interface between technology and society. Precedents are claimed from antiquity, but the modern genre arose in the 19th and early 20th centuries. [[Mary Shelley]]'s *Frankenstein*, written in 1818, is often credited as the first true science fiction novel. [[Jules Verne]] and [[H. G. Wells]] were pivotal figures. The Golden Age of the 20th century added space operas, dystopian literature and pulp magazines. The genre has also influenced film and television, and it can criticize present-day society while inspiring a sense of wonder.

Weekly peer-reviewed [[Academic journal|academic journal]] of the American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS), first published in 1880. Based in the District of Columbia, with a second office in Cambridge, England, it has a subscriber base of around 130,000 and an estimated readership of over 400,000. Unlike most scientific journals, *Science* and its rival *Nature* cover the full range of scientific disciplines. Its 2024 impact factor was 45.8, and fewer than 7% of submitted articles are accepted. It was founded by John Michels with financial support from [[Thomas Edison]] and [[Alexander Graham Bell]], and ended publication in March 1882. It became the journal of the AAAS in 1900. Early papers included work by [[Albert Einstein]] on gravitational lensing and by [[Edwin Hubble]] on spiral nebulae.

American popular science magazine, the oldest continuously published magazine in the United States. It was founded in 1845 by inventor and publisher Rufus Porter as a four-page weekly newspaper, and its early issues reported on patents and inventions. Scientists including [[Albert Einstein]] and [[Nikola Tesla]] once contributed articles, and more than 150 [[Nobel Prize]] winners have been featured since its inception. It became a monthly in 1921. After World War II it was revived in 1948 by three partners who bought its assets. Under editor in chief Laura Helmuth, hired in 2020, it shifted toward politics. Owned by Springer Nature until June 2026, it was sold that month to LabX Media Group.

Statement based on repeated experiments or observations that describes or predicts a range of natural phenomena. Laws are developed from data, are often expressed mathematically, and are directly or indirectly based on empirical evidence. Unlike a [[Theory|scientific theory]], a law does not posit a mechanism; it summarizes results within a certain range of application. [[Ohm's law]] applies only to linear networks, [[Newton's law of universal gravitation|Newton's law of gravitation]] only in weak gravitational fields, and [[Hooke's law]] only to strain below the elastic limit. Many laws take equation form, such as the law of conservation of energy, written ΔE = 0. Laws may be contradicted, restricted or extended by future observations. They differ from hypotheses, which have not been verified to the same degree.

Activity of producing models of empirical objects, phenomena and physical processes, to make part of the world easier to understand, quantify, visualize or simulate. It requires selecting the relevant features of a real situation and building a model that replicates them. Conceptual, operational, mathematical, computational and graphical models serve different purposes. Models are typically used when direct experimental measurement is impossible or impractical, although direct measurement under controlled conditions is more reliable. [[John von Neumann]] wrote that the sciences mainly make models, justified if they are expected to describe phenomena from a reasonably wide area. A model is task-driven, leaving out details unimportant to the task and [[Abstraction|abstracting]] others. Scientific debate often concerns which model is better for a given task, such as seasonal climate forecasting.

Way of expressing numbers too large or too small to write conveniently in decimal form, as a coefficient multiplied by a power of ten. In normalized form, the coefficient is usually between 1 and 10 in absolute value and the exponent is an integer, so 350 is written as 3.5 × 10². It is also called scientific form, or standard form in the United Kingdom. Scientists, mathematicians and engineers use it widely, partly because it simplifies arithmetic and comparison of magnitudes. Engineering notation restricts the exponent to multiples of three to match SI prefixes, so 12.5 × 10⁻⁹ m can be written as 12.5 nm. [[Calculator|Calculators]] and computer programs typically display it in E notation, and decimal floating point is closely related.

Explanation of an aspect of the natural world that has been repeatedly tested and corroborated in accordance with the [[Scientific method|scientific method]]. A theory connects and explains multiple observations, and it is expected to make predictions that further observations could confirm or refute. A [[Fact|fact]] is a single observation, while a theory differs from a [[Scientific law|law]], which describes a relationship without explaining it. In everyday speech a theory can mean an unsubstantiated guess, but in science it usually refers to a well-tested explanation. A theory's strength depends on the diversity of phenomena it explains and its simplicity, and it may be modified or rejected if it cannot fit new findings. Some, such as evolution, heliocentric theory and [[Plate tectonics|plate tectonics]], are so well established that they are unlikely to change fundamentally. Hypotheses are said to be supported rather than proven.

Belief system and practices created by American author [[L. Ron Hubbard|L. Ron Hubbard]]. Hubbard presented his ideas in 1950 as a talk therapy called Dianetics, later reframed them as a religion, and in 1953 founded the Church of Scientology. A core belief is that traumatic events leave subconscious recordings that can be relieved only through auditing, for which fees are charged. Advancement through levels such as Clear and Operating Thetan is structured. By one 2014 estimate the church had around 30,000 members. It has been described variously as a [[Religion|religion]], a [[Cult|cult]], a business and a scam.

Roman general and statesman, one of the main architects of Rome's victory over Carthage in the Second Punic War. Born into a patrician family, he survived the Roman defeat at [[Battle of Cannae|Cannae]] in 216 BC. In 210 BC, although he had never held consular office, he was elected to command Rome's forces in [[Iberian Peninsula|Hispania]], where he won at Ilipa in 206 BC. Elected consul in 205 BC, he invaded Carthage's African homeland, compelling Carthage to recall [[Hannibal]]. His victory over Hannibal at Zama in 202 BC ended the war and earned him the epithet Africanus, meaning "the African". Despite his triumphs he had many political opponents, notably [[Cato the Elder]]. In 187 BC he and his brother faced trials for bribes allegedly received from the Seleucid king Antiochus III, after which he left Rome for his villa at Liternum.

Hand-operated cutting [[Tool|tool]] made of two pivoting blades whose sharpened edges slide past each other when the handles are squeezed. Scissors cut thin materials such as paper, cardboard, cloth, rope and wire. Heavy-duty scissors for tough materials are usually called shears, and larger two-handed implements are called trimmers. The right type matters: hair-cutting shears have blade angles suited to heaped bundles of hair, while kitchen shears are designed for tough foods such as [[Meat|meat]], [[Tendon|tendon]] and [[Bone|bone]]. Surgical scissors divide [[Tissue (biology)|tissue]] and trim implants. Most have ringed handles, and some have a [[Spring (device)|spring]] between the blades to assist opening. Pivoted scissors became common in northwest Europe during the 13th and 14th centuries, and the Hangzhou Zhang Xiaoquan Company has made them since 1663.

Medical condition in which the spine has an irregular, usually S- or C-shaped curve in the coronal plane, often with rotation. Mild curves rarely cause problems, but severe cases can affect breathing and movement. The cause is usually unknown, with genetic and environmental factors believed to contribute. It often appears during growth spurts before [[Puberty|puberty]] and can also result from [[Cerebral palsy|cerebral palsy]]. Diagnosis is confirmed with [[X-ray|X-rays]]. Minor curves are watched, while bracing, exercise or surgery may be used. It occurs in about 3% of people, most commonly between ages ten and twenty, and affects females more severely, at a ratio of 4:1.

American media franchise created in 1969 by Joe Ruby and Ken Spears for [[Hanna-Barbera]], with the animated series *Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!* It follows four teenagers and their talking Great Dane, who solve mysteries involving supposedly supernatural creatures while traveling in a van called the Mystery Machine. The original series aired on [[CBS|CBS]] from 1969 to 1976, then on ABC. Later reboots appeared on [[Cartoon Network|Cartoon Network]], and two aired on Kids' WB on The WB and its successor [[The CW|The CW]]. Hanna-Barbera was absorbed into Warner Bros. Animation in 2001. In 2013, TV Guide ranked the series the fifth-greatest TV cartoon of all time.

Tropane alkaloid and muscarinic antagonist, also known as hyoscine, used to treat motion sickness and postoperative nausea and vomiting. It is sometimes given before [[Surgery|surgery]] to reduce saliva. When injected, its effects begin after about 20 minutes and last up to eight hours. It is the main active component of certain [[Solanaceae|nightshade]] plants, which have been used as deliriants, since higher doses cause hallucinations. Scopolamine was first described in 1881 and came into use for [[Anesthesia|anesthesia]] around 1900. It is not recommended in people with angle-closure [[Glaucoma|glaucoma]] or bowel obstruction.

Diverse order of [[Actinopterygii|ray-finned fishes]], including the stonefish, [[Lionfish|lionfish]] and sculpins, with over 1,320 species, making it one of the five largest orders of bony fishes. They are known as mail-cheeked fishes because a bony suborbital stay extends across the cheek to the preoperculum. Most are carnivorous bottom-dwellers in shallow water that feed on crustaceans and smaller fish, although some live in deep or fresh water. Most species are under 30 cm (12 in) long, but the skilfish can reach 183 cm (6.00 ft). Classification is unsettled, with accounts ranging from 26 to 35 families. The suborder Scorpaenoidei includes the sea robins and the scorpionfishes, which, according to Minouri Ishida's 1994 work and recent studies, have twelve families.

Predatory [[Arachnid|arachnid]] order with eight legs, a pair of grasping pincers and a narrow, segmented tail ending in a stinger. Scorpions have existed since the [[Silurian|Silurian]] Period, about 430 million years ago, and live on every continent except [[Antarctica|Antarctica]]. Most inhabit deserts, although they have adapted to a wide range of environments. Over 2,500 species are described, in 22 living families. They mainly prey on [[Insect|insects]] and other [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]], restraining prey with their pincers and killing it with venom, though some species hunt vertebrates. All known species give live birth, and mothers carry their young on their backs. Their exoskeletons contain fluorescent chemicals that glow under [[Ultraviolet|ultraviolet]] light. About 25 species have venom capable of killing a human.

German hard rock and heavy metal band formed in [[Hanover]] in 1965 by guitarist Rudolf Schenker. Its best-known line-up, from 1978 to 1992, included vocalist Klaus Meine, lead guitarist Matthias Jabs, bassist Francis Buchholz and drummer Herman Rarebell. The band is estimated to have sold more than 100 million records. Its single "Wind of Change" became a symbol of the political changes in Eastern Europe and the [[Fall of the Berlin Wall|fall of the Berlin Wall]], and has sold over 14 million copies. The Scorpions became the first heavy metal band from a non-English-speaking country to achieve international success.

Zodiac constellation in the southern celestial hemisphere, between Libra to the west and [[Sagittarius (constellation)|Sagittarius]] to the east. It sits near the center of the [[Milky Way|Milky Way]], and its recognition predates Greek culture. It is one of the 48 constellations identified by [[Ptolemy|Ptolemy]] in the second century. Its bright stars include [[Antares|Antares]], a reddish star known as "rival of Mars". Messier 4 and Messier 80 are among its globular clusters, and U Scorpii is the fastest known [[Nova|nova]]. In classical myth, the giant scorpion and its enemy Orion became constellations on opposite sides of the sky.
